rewritten_text: I thought this charming falsehood was told with grace and simplicity, though perhaps its novelty for me was the reason; it had surely delighted the others when first heard. Sir Dinadan the Humorist stirred first, waking the group with a crude prank. He fastened metal cups to a dog's tail and released the panicked animal, which bolted through the room followed by a pack of barking dogs, causing a chaotic, deafening uproar. The crowd roared with laughter, some falling from their seats and rolling on the ground in delight, acting much like children. Dinadan, immensely proud, recounted the origin of his inspiration repeatedly until everyone grew weary, yet he continued to chuckle long after the others had ceased. He then insisted on delivering a humorous speech, which consisted of the most tiresome, exhausted jests I had ever endured. He was more tedious than any minstrel or circus clown. It was melancholy to sit there, thirteen centuries before my own time, hearing the same stale, ancient jokes that had irritated me as a boy in the future. It confirmed my suspicion that no truly original joke exists. Everyone laughed at these relics, as people always do, though the boy did not; he mocked them, declaring most of Dinadan's humor rotten and the rest fossilized. I remarked that 'fossilized' was apt, as I felt those jokes could only be categorized by geologic eras. The boy was confused, as geology had not yet been conceived, but I recorded the thought, intending to teach the public once I had the chance. One should not discard a clever idea simply because the time is not yet right. Then, Sir Kay stood and began to spin his tales, using me as his subject.

I wonder how long you would have waited if left to yourself, or if you would have spoken at all without my prompting. My decision to thank you for helping Lydia had a strong effect—perhaps too much. If our happiness comes from breaking a promise, what happens to the moral of the story? I should not have brought it up. This is not right. You need not worry. The moral remains sound. Lady Catherine’s attempts to keep us apart actually cleared away my doubts. My current happiness does not depend on your gratitude; I was already determined to know the truth after hearing from my aunt. Lady Catherine has been useful, which should please her. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it just to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward, or did you have a more serious goal? My true purpose was to see you and decide if I could hope for your love. My stated goal was to see if your sister still cared for Bingley, and if so, to tell him what I have since confessed. Will you have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is happening? I am more likely to need time than courage, Elizabeth. It must be done, and if you give me paper, I will do it now. If I did not have my own letter to write, I might sit and admire your handwriting, as someone else once did. But I have an aunt I have neglected for too long. Because she did not want to admit how much her closeness to Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner. Now, having news she knew would be welcome, she felt guilty that her aunt and uncle had missed out on three days of happiness and wrote immediately: My dear aunt, I should have thanked you sooner for your kind letter, but I was too annoyed to write. You assumed more than was true. Now, however, you may imagine whatever you like. Let your fancy run wild; unless you believe I am already married, you cannot be far from the truth.

Tom joined the Cadets of Temperance, drawn by their flashy uniforms. He pledged to avoid smoking, chewing tobacco, and swearing while a member. He quickly discovered that promising to abstain only made him crave those very things. His urge to drink and curse became so intense that only the prospect of wearing his red sash kept him in the group. He looked forward to a grand public funeral for the dying Judge Frazer, but the Judge kept recovering. Tom grew frustrated and resigned, only for the Judge to die that same night. Tom felt betrayed by the man's inconsistency. The funeral was impressive, and the Cadets marched in a way that would have made Tom jealous, but he was relieved to be free. Surprisingly, once he was allowed to drink and swear again, he lost all interest in doing so. Soon, Tom found his newfound freedom boring. He tried keeping a diary, but gave up after three days of inactivity. A traveling minstrel show arrived, and Tom and Joe Harper organized their own troupe, enjoying it for two days. Even the Fourth of July was a letdown; it rained, canceling the parade, and the visiting U.S. Senator, Mr. Benton, was a massive disappointment because he was nowhere near the twenty-five feet tall Tom had imagined. Then, a circus came to town.

He would never have escaped without my help. Morgan le Fay hated him deeply and would never have shown him mercy. His crime was mostly thoughtless, though; he had simply mentioned her red hair. While true, it was a social blunder, as people of her status are said to have auburn hair. Consider that among these forty-seven prisoners, five had been forgotten entirely. These elderly, frail people could no longer recall their own names or why they were imprisoned. The priests who visited them only taught them to accept their suffering as God's will, and even their records were lost. We only knew they had been locked away for at least thirty-five years. The king and queen viewed them as mere inherited property, like old furniture, and never thought to release them. When I asked the queen why they remained, she was puzzled; the idea of freeing them had never occurred to her. To her, they were simply assets, and people rarely discard property even when it lacks value. I led these human ghosts out into the sunlight, having blindfolded them first to protect their sensitive eyes. They were a tragic sight—skeletal, withered figures who stood as the true legacy of the monarchy and the church.
